scenes.narration: What if most of the giant ships that carry your phone, your clothes and your coffee were registered in countries they almost never visit? And what if that choice of flag decided the rules on board, the taxes the owner pays, and who protects the crew?

They are. According to the United Nations' trade agency, just three flags, Liberia, Panama and the Marshall Islands, carry 45 percent of the world's shipping capacity. Yet the biggest ship owners are Greek, Chinese and Japanese.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: So whose ship is it, really? The answer is stranger than you might think. Let's start with one famous ship.

Every ship must be registered in one country, its flag state. That flag decides which country's laws apply on board: safety rules, labor rules and taxes. It works like the ship's passport. In theory, the flag state is also the one that must inspect the ship and make sure those rules are followed, wherever it sails.

Remember the giant ship that got stuck in the Suez Canal in twenty twenty-one, the Ever Given? It was owned by a Japanese company, operated by a Taiwanese shipping line, flagged in Panama, and stuck in Egypt. One ship, four countries. As the Associated Press put it at the time, matters quickly became an international morass.

And it is not an exception. Greek owners control the biggest share of the world's fleet, about 16 percent of all carrying capacity. Asian companies own more than half of it, European companies about a third. But look at the flags, and the top three are small countries most people could not find on a map. That is true across a world fleet of about 116,000 vessels. Greece, China and Japan together own more than 40 percent of the world's carrying capacity.

scenes.visual_objective: Kinetic typography: lines enter word by word on narration cues
scenes.narration: So how did a few small countries end up flying the world's fleet? It started with a drink.

keyframes.label: How did a few small countries
end up flying the world's fleet?

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: Where did the idea of borrowing another country's flag come from?

In the nineteen twenties, alcohol was banned in the United States. Ship owners who wanted to serve drinks to their passengers found a way out: they registered their ships in Panama. Panama became the first open registry, a flag that anyone, from any country, could fly. And as American shipping laws grew stricter, more and more owners followed them there.

After the Second World War, a historian found, Panama's officials started demanding so much in private payments that ship owners wanted an alternative. In 1948, a former American Secretary of State, Edward Stettinius, worked with the government of Liberia to open a new registry. And to this day, the Liberian registry is run from an office in Virginia, in the United States. That registry would grow into the biggest in the world.

scenes.visual_objective: Kinetic typography: lines enter word by word on narration cues
scenes.narration: The idea spread so fast that it got its own name. In the nineteen fifties, people started calling it a flag of convenience: a flag chosen not for where the ship comes from, but for what it saves. One historian described it more bluntly: a haven from high standards.

keyframes.label: chosen not for where the ship comes from, but for what it saves

scenes.narration: Let me draw how an open registry works. A ship owner in Athens, Shanghai or Tokyo picks a flag from a menu. The registry, often a private company working for the flag country, signs the ship up, collects the fees, and sends part of the money to the government. The ship never has to visit the country at all.

scenes.visual_objective: Kinetic typography: lines enter word by word on narration cues
scenes.narration: A flag you can choose like a product. But why would an owner choose a faraway flag over its own?

keyframes.label: A flag you choose like a product

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: What does a ship owner actually gain? And what does the small country get in return?

According to the maritime analytics firm Windward, owners choose a flag of convenience to escape stricter rules at home, to cut operating costs, to avoid high taxes, and, in the worst cases, to get around the laws that protect sailors' wages and working conditions. Panama, for example, offers registration online and lets owners hire low-cost crews from anywhere.

scenes.visual_objective: Side-by-side figures count up; bars rise
scenes.narration: And it works at an enormous scale. In twenty twenty-six, Liberia became the first registry in history to pass 300 million tons of ships, with about 6,000 ships flying its flag. Liberia alone carries 17 percent of the world's shipping capacity. It says it flies almost a quarter of all the world's container ships, the ones that carry the boxes with your online orders.

keyframes.label: first registry ever to pass it

scenes.narration: So what does Liberia earn? Registration fees, yearly tonnage taxes, inspections and certificates. A local researcher estimates the country's maritime revenue at about 30 million dollars in twenty twenty-six. For a country like Liberia, that matters. But it is a tiny slice of an industry that carries the world's trade. And exactly how much? The researcher says only the registry and Liberia's maritime authority hold the full records, which is why he is calling for more transparency.

scenes.visual_objective: Kinetic typography: lines enter word by word on narration cues
scenes.narration: Cheaper, simpler, lighter rules. But when something goes wrong far out at sea, who is responsible?

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: What happens to the people on board when the owner simply disappears? On paper, the flag state should step in. In practice, it often doesn't.

It happens more and more. According to the International Transport Workers' Federation, about 3,100 sailors were abandoned by their ship owners in twenty twenty-four, up from about 1,700 the year before. Left on board, far from home, often without pay, food or a way back. They were owed more than 20 million dollars in unpaid wages.
In total, 312 ships were abandoned in twenty twenty-four, more than twice as many as the year before. Each one is a crew stuck in a foreign port, waiting for someone to take responsibility.

And 81 percent of the abandoned ships were flying a flag of convenience. When the owner hides behind a company in one country and a flag in another, the crew has almost no one to call. The flag with the most abandoned ships was Panama.

Let me draw why this is so hard to fix. The owner lives in one country. The company that legally owns the ship is registered in a second. The flag belongs to a third. The crew comes from a fourth. And the ship is stuck in the port of a fifth. Each one can say: it's not my problem.

Some ships go further, and fly flags that are not real at all. Researchers at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air counted 113 Russian vessels flying a false flag in the first nine months of twenty twenty-five, often to dodge sanctions on oil. And the shadow fleet keeps finding new homes: six registries that had never flagged a Russian ship before the invasion of Ukraine were flying 162 shadow vessels between them by September.

scenes.visual_objective: Kinetic typography: lines enter word by word on narration cues
scenes.narration: So why doesn't the world simply ban it?

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: If flags of convenience cause so many problems, why do they keep growing? And why does the system survive every scandal?

Because almost everyone gains something. Owners save money. Small countries earn fees. Shipping stays cheap, and so do the goods it carries, all the way to your local store. The world's fleet now carries 2.5 billion tons of cargo capacity, and most of it moves under a flag of choice. Changing that would mean higher costs for owners, less income for small countries, and, in the end, higher prices for everyone.

scenes.visual_objective: Side-by-side figures count up; bars rise
scenes.narration: And the big registries compete hard to look like the safe choice. Liberia says about a quarter of the world's newly built ships are joining its flag. But the list of abandoned ships tells a mixed story: Panama tops it, followed by smaller flags like Palau, Tanzania, Comoros, Cameroon and Bahrain.

scenes.visual_objective: Kinetic typography: lines enter word by word on narration cues
scenes.narration: The real question is not where a ship is registered. It is whether anyone, anywhere, is truly responsible for it. Because a flag is supposed to be a promise: that someone will check the ship, protect the crew, and answer when things go wrong.

keyframes.label: Not where a ship is registered
but whether anyone is truly responsible

scenes.narration: So, next time you see a giant ship on the horizon, look at the back of it. The name of a port will be painted there, Monrovia, Panama or Majuro, far from its owners, its crew and its cargo. A flag that was chosen like a product, for a world that runs on cheap shipping. Three small flags, almost half of the world's shipping capacity, and a question that still has no simple answer: who is really in charge out there?
